Chapter 1. Introduction to MLflow for GenAI on Databricks

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) development teams run into the same problems repeatedly: manually tracking training experiments, struggling to manage models in production, and working without a reliable monitoring stack. These gaps erode reliability, scalability, and reproducibility, and they get worse as projects grow. Managing the ML lifecycle needs a more structured approach.

MLflow was built to close those gaps. Since its first release in June 2018, the open source platform has worked to standardize and streamline ML development by offering solutions for tracking experiments, reproducing training runs, and managing models. Adoption has grown steadily: MLflow reached 10 million monthly downloads in November 2022 and passed 16 million by the end of 2023. Much of that growth comes from its open, flexible design. It integrates with widely used ML libraries and runs reliably across environments, from local machines to cloud platforms.

As enterprises build more generative AI (GenAI) applications with large language models (LLMs), effective lifecycle management becomes increasingly important. Compared to traditional machine learning, GenAI solutions are more complex and require disciplined practices to ensure they are implemented and managed sustainably over the long term.

This chapter introduces the fundamentals of using MLflow on the Databricks platform. It provides an overview of MLflow’s core components and its capabilities for managing the ML lifecycle. After that, we’ll take a look at the evolution from MLflow 2.x to 3.x, compare its open source and Databricks-managed implementations, and specifically address the unique challenges in GenAI development. To conclude, we will introduce the primary use case that will guide our exploration of MLflow’s practical application throughout this book.

What Is MLflow?

MLflow is a popular, open source platform built to help ML and GenAI practitioners in managing and tracking their experiments for reproducibility. You might already be familiar with the MLflow logo, which you can see in Figure 1-1.

MLflow has become a go-to tool for AI/ML developers because it provides a standardized framework for navigating the complexity of the ML lifecycle. Without a structured approach, developers struggle to track experiment runs and model versions across different environments. This leads to inconsistencies, difficulty comparing model performance, and complex deployments. By enabling systematic experiment tracking, reproducible training runs, and centralized model management, MLflow has changed how both individual developers and organizations work.

Experiment and Model Tracking for Reproducibility

MLflow’s tracking capabilities matter most for practitioners who need to systematically log experiments. It automates the recording of hyperparameters, code changes, feature engineering steps, and resulting model performance (Figure 1-2). This makes it easy to identify which combination produced the best results and to understand the impact of changes over time. While we can track this information in a spreadsheet or on paper, a library that logs and stores it automatically streamlines development and reduces manual errors.

Tracking model changes and their downstream impacts can be difficult, especially when testing spans many iterations and long time periods. MLflow makes it easier to compare runs over time and understand what changed, when it changed, and what effect these changes had.

MLflow also supports reproducibility by logging critical information about each training run, enabling consistent re-creation of results. Trustworthy, reproducible models are central to production best practices, particularly in regulated domains such as finance and healthcare, where a complete, auditable model history is often required. Even so, reproducibility can be hard to achieve due to evolving data and the complexity of managing experimental details.

When you train a model with MLflow, it records environment details, including the libraries used and their versions. It also tracks parameters, metrics, code versions, and artifacts such as models and data files, creating a comprehensive record for every experiment. For example, as Figure 1-2 shows, after multiple model versions have been logged over time, you can rerun training or redeploy a prior configuration if the latest version introduces issues or performance regressions later in the development cycle.

For instance, if a run was initiated from a notebook, MLflow logs the notebook version so you can revisit the exact code used for a specific run, even if the code has changed since then. That link to the source code lets you retrace the logic and reexecute steps when needed.

MLflow on Databricks also integrates with Delta Lake, an open source storage layer built on Apache Parquet that adds ACID transactions and schema enforcement. With Delta Lake, you can record the exact version of a dataset used in an experiment run, which makes it practical to reproduce and validate experiments later. That combination of code versioning and data versioning keeps ML workflows consistent and auditable.

MLflow Evaluation

MLflow also provides an evaluation framework for AI and ML workloads. It makes model assessment techniques accessible to teams of all sizes with minimal code. Whether you are prototyping or running enterprise deployments, MLflow’s evaluation tools track model performance in a standardized way so you can compare results and refine with confidence.

One-liner evaluation function

MLflow enables comprehensive model assessment through the mlflow.evaluate() function. This single command runs pretemplated evaluations designed for diverse AI and ML problems, eliminating the need for complex setup procedures.

Beyond measuring only the performance of a model’s final output, MLflow also supports evaluation of diverse steps across the model development pipeline, such as models, functions, or static datasets. This flexibility allows teams to assess different components of their ML pipeline using consistent methodologies and interfaces and pinpoint what component needs to be improved for overall performance.

Figure 1-3 illustrates how the mlflow.evaluate() function passes the model’s predictions to a default evaluator, which then uses built-in metrics to evaluate the problem at hand. These built-in metrics score the validation dataframe passed to the function and return the results as artifacts, which are then stored in the Metrics Store and analysis on the MLflow UI.

Built-in model and artifacts support

The default evaluator in mlflow.evaluate() supports various model types, including classifiers, multiclassifiers, regressors, and GenAI applications such as question-answering chatbots. For each predefined model type, the evaluator automatically selects appropriate metrics and generates relevant artifacts, including model summary plots, feature importance visualizations, and type-specific performance metrics.

The evaluators can be extended to support a wide range of scenarios, such as:

Dataset evaluation

Static datasets and precomputed predictions can be evaluated without rerunning models, making it suitable for batch processing and historical review.

Python and custom function

Functions can be evaluated directly, without the need for model logging or registration.

Custom evaluation metrics

Business requirements can be met by defining custom evaluation criteria, metrics, and visualizations tailored to specific domains.

SHAP integration

SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values provide model interpretability, including feature importance, SHAP value analysis, and explainable AI for transparent machine learning.

Specialized plug-ins

Evaluation capabilities can be extended with specialized plug-ins, such as Giskard for vulnerability assessment and Trubrics for enhanced validation.

These capabilities can be used for more specific or complex use cases. Because MLflow offers custom metrics capabilities, teams can define domain-specific evaluation criteria using metric builders catered to their exact use case. This extensibility ensures that unique business requirements and AI/ML problems are all supported within the evaluation framework.

Evaluation analysis

MLflow provides strong capabilities for visualizing and comparing model runs, making it easier to select the best-performing run. Rather than simply storing raw metrics, MLflow offers an interactive UI (Figure 1-4) for exploring and analyzing performance across experiments.

Its evaluation framework stores results in a structured format that supports visualization, deeper analysis, and sharing across teams. Through the MLflow interface, team members can review evaluation outcomes together, compare models side by side, and make decisions using a transparent, auditable Artifact Repository, available for process.

Collaboration

ML model development often starts locally, which gives practitioners flexibility and fast feedback during experimentation. That setup becomes a problem when teams need to collaborate, especially as projects scale or move toward production.

MLflow addresses that collaboration gap by creating an accessible central repository to share and store model experiments and artifacts, regardless of where the experiment was initiated. It is a practical way to unify a team using different tools and platforms for AI and ML development, since the MLflow tracking server can be reached from any code editor using the REST API or Python SDK. Figure 1-5 illustrates multiple options.

Model Registry and Versioning

As ML projects scale, teams often struggle to manage numerous model versions without a central system. This lack of a single source of truth makes it difficult to track data lineage, leads to confusion when selecting models for production, and creates significant deployment and governance bottlenecks.

Using the MLflow Model Registry offers the following benefits:

Version control

The registry automatically tracks versions of each model, allowing teams to compare iterations, roll back to previous states, and manage multiple versions in parallel (e.g., staging versus production).

Model lineage and traceability

Each registered model version is linked to the MLflow run, logged model, or notebook that produced it, enabling full reproducibility. We can trace back exactly how a model was trained, with what data and parameters.

Production-ready workflows

Features like model aliases (e.g., @champion) and tags make it easier to manage deployment workflows, promoting models to experimental, staging, or production environments in a controlled and auditable way.

Governance and compliance

With structured metadata, tagging, and role-based access controls (when used with a backend like Databricks or a managed MLflow service), the MLflow Model Registry supports governance requirements critical for enterprise-grade ML operations.

What we have now is a dedicated model registry for governing and managing models, rather than an object store cluttered with lots of model files.

Core MLflow Components: Experiments, Runs, and Model Registry

Now that we have an idea of what MLflow does, let’s walk through its main components and how they interact with one another.

MLflow experiment

Using MLflow starts with creating an experiment. An experiment is the primary unit for organizing and tracking model development runs. It acts as a container for related runs, allowing us to group runs together for a specific model, task, or project (Figure 1-6).

MLflow run

In MLflow, there’s also the concept of runs. Each run is encapsulated in an experiment and is used to specifically track one model-training execution by logging its parameters, metrics, and artifacts so that it’s easier to compare results in the future. A run can contain:

  • Model metadata (e.g., parameters, hyperparameters)

  • Model artifacts (e.g., pickle files)

  • Model metrics (e.g., f1 score for training, validation, testing, etc.)

  • Library requirements and package dependencies

These resources are stored in the artifacts section of the run and can be retrieved for assessment or to reproduce the model for testing or audit (Figure 1-7).

MLflow Model Registry

Once a model run has produced a satisfactory model, we can register that model into the registry. Registering a validated model in the MLflow Model Registry transitions it from an experimental asset to a production-ready candidate. Think of this registry as a central hub that systematically versions models for deployment and maintains a complete history for management and auditability.

The MLflow Model Registry provides the critical link between model experimentation and production deployment. For enterprise environments, the Databricks Model Registry adds more granular governance, enabling fine-grained access privileges for permitted user groups across the entire lifecycle of models and experiments. Figure 1-8 illustrates how successful model runs are registered within the MLflow Model Registry.

We’ll talk more about the specific differences in implementation techniques in “Open Source Versus Databricks Implementations”. Before we delve into those specifics, let’s explore the big updates in going from MLflow 2.x to MLflow 3.x, and why they matter for us.

From MLflow 2.x to MLflow 3.x

While MLflow was mainly known as a platform for managing the ML lifecycle, the rise of GenAI applications made it necessary to update existing capabilities for more efficient GenAI management. The upgrade from MLflow 2.x to MLflow 3.x is mainly focused around supporting GenAI features to deliver improved experiment tracking, observability, and performance evaluation. While MLflow 3.x introduces significant new capabilities, it still preserves its core concepts. Among the many new features, let’s touch on a few highlights next.

Advanced GenAI evaluation

MLflow 3.x introduces the mlflow.genai.evaluate() function to assess GenAI applications. It supports methods such as LLM-as-a-judge to score traces, along with built-in metrics commonly used in GenAI evaluation, including safety, relevance, and correctness. It also supports collecting human feedback, which remains the gold standard for evaluating GenAI applications.

Comprehensive tracing

MLflow 3.x provides enhanced end-to-end tracing for complex GenAI applications, allowing developers to debug and monitor the behavior of each subcomponent such as LLM calls, database retrieval, and external API requests. This enables detailed performance analysis and improved observability across the entire application workflow.

These features help solve the similar challenges that practitioners face with traditional ML models, but they are now geared for the more complex world of GenAI applications where quality assessment can be much more subjective and harder to measure systematically.

Open Source Versus Databricks Implementations

Open source MLflow and the Databricks-managed version are largely similar in functionality. Databricks offers a fully managed MLflow experience that removes the need to operate the underlying infrastructure and adds an enterprise-grade governance layer on top of the open source capabilities. Both use the same MLflow library, so we can take advantage of Databricks-specific benefits without being locked into a single vendor.

Overview on Databricks workspace and Unity Catalog

There are a few Databricks terms that need explaining before we look at the main differences between open source MLflow and managed MLflow on Databricks:

Databricks workspace

The Databricks workspace is a Databricks deployment in a cloud service account. It provides a unified environment for working with Databricks assets for a specified set of users.

Databricks Unity Catalog

Databricks Unity Catalog (UC) is a centralized data and AI catalog that provides access control, auditing, lineage, quality monitoring, and discovery capabilities across Databricks workspaces.

Key features of UC include:

Define it once and secure it everywhere

This offers a single place to administer data access policies that apply across all workspaces in a region.

Standards-compliant security model

This model is based on standard ANSI SQL and allows administrators to grant permissions in their existing data lake using familiar syntax.

Built-in auditing and lineage

This includes user-level audit logs that automatically record how users access and use assets on the platform. It also captures lineage data that tracks how data assets are created and used across all languages.

Data discovery

Tagging and documentation of data assets is provided out of the box, along with a search interface to help data consumers find data.

System tables

These help easily access and query all operational data processed in the Databricks platform, including audit logs, billable usage, and lineage.

Workspaces can be bound to multiple catalogs to have access to different data assets with specified governance. In the following example (Figure 1-9), we have three workspaces:

  • A production workspace for data engineering

  • A production workspace for analytics

  • A workspace for development purposes

We can bind both the production workspaces to the same catalog so that they share the production data assets, while the development workspace has access to development data assets and is isolated from production (Figure 1-9).

Models in Unity Catalog extend the benefits of Unity Catalog to ML models, including centralized access control, auditing, lineage, and model discovery across workspaces. Think of Unity Catalog as a universal librarian for all our data and AI assets across every Databricks workspace. It doesn’t matter which team created a dataset or model; the librarian knows where it is, who has permission to access it, and its entire history (lineage).

In Figure 1-9, if the Data Science team creates a model in production and stores it into the production catalog (prod_catalog), that makes the model accessible for other workspaces as well, such as the Production Analytics workspace, that might need access to what the Data Science team created for adding its results in dashboards. The UC Model Registry bridges the gap between teams and environments, easing collaboration by sharing assets across workspaces.

Key differences

With an understanding of Databricks workspaces and UC, we can now take a closer look at the differences between open source MLflow and Databricks-managed MLflow.

Enterprise-grade governance with Unity Catalog

While open source MLflow needs to be self-hosted and doesn’t provide any governance layer, using MLflow integrated within the Databricks platform provides full traceability, monitoring, and unified governance across AI and ML workloads without any setup. This is thanks to Databricks UC, where we can enforce granular access controls and track lineage of models and data. In practice, that means standardized governance controls and easier multiworkspace collaboration out of the box.

Model registry from MLflow server to Databricks Unity Catalog

Another major difference in using MLflow on Databricks is the location of the model registry. The model registry is stored in UC when using Databricks, making it easy to access models across the platform in different workspaces or even locally.

When using the open source tracking server, an MLflow server needs to be deployed (whether locally or on a virtual server) and to share access across collaborators, for which proper infrastructure needs to be designed and maintained. Databricks manages this and hosts the server within the platform, making the use of MLflow collaborative out of the box, with the extra layer of governance and access control (Figure 1-10).

Unified UI and model lifecycle

The managed version of MLflow is integrated into the Databricks platform and unifies ML, deep learning, and GenAI development directly in the platform user interface.

From experiment tracking to deployment, Databricks offers a unified UI for model registry, model versioning, prompt management, and packaging across models and agents, eliminating the need to stitch together separate tools to visualize the end-to-end lifecycle of ML and GenAI projects. Figure 1-11 shows an example.

Note

Since this book’s goal is to focus on the use of MLflow on the Databricks platform, we’ll concentrate on the managed version of MLflow throughout the rest of the chapters.

Tracing and observability

Open source MLflow gives you the tracing data model and APIs as well as integrations like OpenTelemetry and simple autologging so you can record inputs/outputs, spans, and metadata for LLM and agent runs. On the Databricks side, MLflow adds the production pieces: high-volume, autoscaled trace ingestion; built-in production monitoring with dashboards/alerts; and Delta Lakehouse integration so all traces land as Delta tables that you can query with SQL or wire into a conversational chatbot.

Why MLflow for GenAI?

The latest MLflow developments combine tracing and AI-powered tools to help us measure and improve GenAI applications throughout their lifecycle.

Management of Iterative Prompts and Models

GenAI development is a highly iterative process of refining prompts, tweaking model parameters, and swapping out different LLM providers. MLflow provides a structured way to track the specific combination of a prompt, its configuration, and the model that produced a given result. This simplifies reproducing successful outcomes, comparing experiments systematically, and maintaining a clear development lineage.

In the 3.x versions, MLflow can handle unique artifacts of GenAI—not just models but also the prompts and configurations associated with them. The MLflow Prompt Registry extends MLflow’s core functionality. It acts as a centralized repository for prompt templates, with Git-inspired, commit-based versioning; support for side-by-side comparison of prompt versions; and the use of aliases for flexible testing.

GenAI Application End-to-End Observability

Multistep GenAI applications like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic systems are often difficult to debug due to a lack of transparency into their execution flow. MLflow Tracing addresses this by providing end-to-end observability, capturing the entire chain of events to help pinpoint performance bottlenecks and unexpected behavior. This gives a comprehensive visualization of the chain of events when calling the system and helps pinpoint performance bottlenecks, unexpected behavior, and support compliance by maintaining a complete record of every interaction (Figure 1-12). With traces, you are able to see all the intermediate steps when querying a GenAI application, such as tool calls, LLM calls, and final outputs.

MLflow Tracing automatically records every step, including all inputs, outputs, and metadata, creating a detailed audit trail of how an output was generated. These traces can be stored for later audit, validation, or analysis purposes.

Automated Quality Evaluation with LLM-As-a-Judge

Evaluating the quality of GenAI applications is notoriously difficult; traditional metrics often fail because outputs are free-form, a single prompt can yield many valid responses, and manual evaluation is slow, expensive, and subjective.

The LLM-as-a-judge method uses one language model to grade the responses generated by another. Instead of a human reviewing each response for accuracy, relevance, and coherence, an LLM judge scores them automatically. This lets developers validate new application versions faster than manual review allows, while still measuring the qualities that matter.

MLflow introduced evaluation support for LLM-as-a-judge to standardize quality assessment. These judges are specialized LLMs trained to evaluate GenAI outputs against specific quality criteria, providing a score and a detailed rationale for their assessment. When needed, you can also customize this by choosing what LLM to use as a judge, or what metrics to evaluate. This makes it possible to measure metrics that are specific to your use cases, such as intent recognition or factual correctness, ensuring that automated evaluations align with the model’s goal.

Warning

When using an LLM-as-a-judge to evaluate responses, the scores it produces are not absolute or perfectly reliable. Because LLM generations are nondeterministic, the same evaluation can sometimes produce slightly different scores across runs or could hallucinate in some instances. These results should therefore be viewed as helpful signals rather than definitive measurements of quality. For important decisions, it’s often best to combine them with human review or repeated evaluations.

Continuous Improvement from Production Feedback

In a real-world setting, GenAI applications often fail because user questions and usage of chatbots are unpredictable and diverse. A critical challenge is creating a tight feedback loop between the production environment and the development cycle to capture user interactions and feedback.

MLflow helps with this by collecting traces from the deployed application, along with user feedback like thumbs up/down and written feedback. These are collected and can be analyzed to identify problematic interactions or low-quality responses and even be used for automatic evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge, as described earlier.

These real-world examples are then used to curate high-quality evaluation datasets that developers can leverage to test new versions of the application against those datasets, improve performance before redeploying, and ensure that improvements are guided by actual user experience.

Introducing the Book’s Core Use Case

Since this book is meant to guide and provide the best practices to tackle GenAI projects with MLflow and Databricks, let us introduce the main use case that we will follow in the rest of the book to demonstrate MLflow best practices for GenAI.

Our use case will focus on developing a chatbot customer assistant for the mock airline “Unity Airways.” This chatbot’s goal is to help customers with actions such as booking, rescheduling, or canceling their flight reservations. Travelers can also ask questions about airline lounge access, airline policies, baggage allowances, refund rules, or disruption waivers.

To replicate most GenAI projects found in the professional industry, our dataset will contain both structured data (booking records) and unstructured data (frequently asked questions in PDF format):

  • The booking records dataset (Table 1-1) stores all reservation details, journey segments, contact information, fare policies, payment, and refund data for fast booking management and customer support.

  • The FAQ dataset provides categorized questions and answers covering airline policies, services, and rules for instant chatbot reference.

Some key requirements for our use case that we’ll discuss over the span of the book include:

  • To be able to integrate our GenAI agent with diverse data sources. Using our dataset but also online tools to retrieve information, we’re looking to integrate textual data and tabular data.

  • To be able to measure performance across all steps of our solution and pinpoint where performance could be improved.

  • To properly track and govern our development lifecycle for best practice development flow and ease of collaboration through MLflow.

The goal of this use case, more than the business value it derives, is to demonstrate best practices of using MLflow on Databricks for GenAI workloads.

Conclusion and Key Takeaways

In this chapter, we explored the fundamental challenges of the modern machine learning lifecycle, from disorganized experiments to the complex demands of generative AI. We’ve established MLflow as a central tool for bringing structure, reproducibility, and governance to this process.

You should now have a solid understanding of MLflow’s core components and a clear picture of why its latest features are critical for building reliable GenAI applications. With the foundation set and our Unity Airways use case introduced, we are ready to get started. The next chapter will guide you through the complete end-to-end lifecycle of a GenAI project using MLflow on Databricks.
